--- title: 19 Land cover statistics toc-title: In this lesson --- In January 2025, the Eaton and Palisades fires burned through Los Angeles County, where wildlands meet neighborhoods. What was on the ground before the fires? How much of the burned area was trees, shrubs and grasses, and how much was buildings and roads? In this lesson we answer these questions by combining the fire perimeters with a land cover map from the Microsoft Planetary Computer. Along the way, we'll see why we need to check a dataset's CRS before calculating any area. By the end of this lesson, students will be able to: - search a STAC catalog by bounding box and date, and check that the item they selected is the right one, - clip a large raster to a polygon efficiently, - tell categorical from continuous rasters, and plot a categorical raster with one color per class and a legend, - check a dataset's CRS from the data itself and decide whether it is suitable for calculating areas, and - calculate the area and percentage covered by each land cover class within a polygon. ## About the data In this lesson we will use three datasets. The first one is the [10 m Annual Land Use Land Cover (9-class) V2 maps](https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/dataset/io-lulc-annual-v02) produced by Impact Observatory, Microsoft and Esri from Sentinel-2 imagery @impact_observatory_io_lulc_2023. This is a categorical raster with a 10 m x 10 m pixel resolution and one map per year from 2017 to 2023. We will access this data through the [Microsoft Planetary Computer (MPC) data catalog](https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/dataset/io-lulc-annual-v02). The second dataset is the perimeters of the Eaton and Palisades fires, which burned in Los Angeles County in January 2025. The third dataset is a shapefile with the California state boundary, from the US Census Bureau's 2016 TIGER/Line shapefiles @us_census_bureau_tiger_2016. We will only use it to see where the land cover raster sits relative to the fire perimeters. We will also use a CSV file with the code, name and official color of each land cover class. We made it from the raster's metadata and the MPC's class map. The [last section of this lesson](#class-labels-from-the-items-metadata) shows how to get this information from the data itself. :::{.callout-tip appearance="minimal"} Download the following from the [course's Google Drive]({{< var shared-data-folder >}}) and add them to a `data` directory next to your notebook: - `Eaton_Perimeter_20250121`, - `Palisades_Perimeter_20250121`, - `ca_state_boundary`, and - `io-lulc-9-class-labels.csv`. The land cover raster is accessed through the MPC catalog, so there's nothing to download for it. ::: ## Fire perimeter preparation Let's start by importing the necessary libraries: ::: {#8044fe06 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import os import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import matplotlib.patches as mpatches import geopandas as gpd import rioxarray as rioxr from shapely import box import pystac_client import planetary_computer from IPython.display import Image ``` ::: Then import the Eaton Fire perimeter: ::: {#c7920f18 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} eaton = gpd.read_file(os.path.join('data', 'Eaton_Perimeter_20250121', 'Eaton_Perimeter_20250121.shp') ) # Examine fire perimeter data print(eaton.crs) print(eaton.shape) eaton.plot() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` EPSG:3857 (20, 5) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-17-raster-wrangling_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-2.png){width=588 height=393} ::: ::: Notice the perimeter is not a single polygon: it is made of several "Heat Perimeter" polygons. That's fine for what we'll do, since we'll use all of them together. We'll also import the CSV with the land cover class codes, names and colors. We'll use it later in the lesson: ::: {#2b0c7c76 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} labels = pd.read_csv(os.path.join('data', 'io-lulc-9-class-labels.csv')) ``` ::: ## Catalog search Our goal is to retrieve the land cover data over the fire perimeter. In the [last lesson](/book/chapters/lesson-16-STAC.qmd) we used a GeoJSON-type dictionary to do the catalog search. Here we will use a list `[xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax]` with the coordinate values defining the edges of the region we want to search data over. Just as with the GeoJSON, these coordinates have to be in the EPSG:4326 CRS. Our bounding box will come from the Eaton Fire perimeter. Notice we use method chaining to reproject and extract the bounds. ::: {#3cc63353 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Create list of bounding box coords for search in 4326 CRS eaton_bbox = list(eaton.to_crs('epsg:4326') .total_bounds ) eaton_bbox ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=100} ``` [-118.16206999988188, 34.16189200012067, -118.01305200016513, 34.23783206465605] ``` ::: ::: Next, we connect to the Microsoft Planetary Computer data catalog and perform the search. The collection ID for this land cover data is `io-lulc-annual-v02`. This collection has one map per year, so we also need to choose a year. The fires happened in January 2025 and the most recent map is for 2023, so we'll search for 2023: ::: {#9711785c .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Open MPC data catalog catalog = pystac_client.Client.open( "https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1", modifier=planetary_computer.sign_inplace, ) # Search MPC catalog search = catalog.search(collections=['io-lulc-annual-v02'], bbox=eaton_bbox, datetime='2023') # Retrieve search items items = search.item_collection() print(f"Returned {len(items)} Items") items ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Returned 2 Items ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=101} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Notice that `band` is a dimension of length 1. `rioxarray` always adds a `band` dimension, even when the raster has a single band. Removing it leaves a two-dimensional array with only `y` and `x`, which matches what the data is and makes it simpler to index and to pass to other functions. We'll also check the raster's data type and CRS: ::: {#52bc236c .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Remove length 1 dimension (band) and its coordinate lulc = lulc.squeeze('band', drop=True) print("Sizes of dimensions:", dict(lulc.sizes)) print("Data type:", lulc.dtype) print("CRS:", lulc.rio.crs) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sizes of dimensions: {'y': 89162, 'x': 56684} Data type: uint8 CRS: EPSG:32611 ``` ::: ::: Next, let's look at how the raster is located with respect to the Eaton Fire perimeter and the CA state boundary: ::: {#5198f9c6 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Create GeoDataFrame from raster bounding box lulc_bbox = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry = [box(*lulc.rio.bounds())], crs = lulc.rio.crs) ca = gpd.read_file(os.path.join('data', 'ca_state_boundary', 'ca_state_boundary.shp')) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # Plot raster boundary, fire perimeter, and CA boundary fig, ax = plt.subplots() ca.plot(ax=ax, color='white', edgecolor ='black') # Reproject lulc_bbox and fire perimeter to match CA crs lulc_bbox.to_crs(ca.crs).plot(ax=ax, alpha=0.3) eaton.to_crs(ca.crs).plot(ax=ax, color='red') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-17-raster-wrangling_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){width=374 height=411} ::: ::: We can see the raster covers a big area relative to the fire perimeter. Since we want to calculate the land cover statistics within the fire perimeter, we will have to clip the raster to this area. ## Clip raster to geometry Before clipping, let's check the raster's no-data value, since `rio.clip()` will use it to fill the pixels outside the fire perimeter: ::: {#f40aadbe .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} print('No-data value: ', lulc.rio.nodata) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` No-data value: 0 ``` ::: ::: The raster already has a no-data value, 0, so we don't need to set one ourselves. We'll look at what each code means in a moment. In our [first lesson about rasters](/book/chapters/lesson-15-rioxarray/lesson-15-rioxarray.qmd) we saw how to clip a raster to a rectangular region. In our case, we want to clip the raster exactly to the fire perimeter. Clipping can be a costly operation for such a big raster relative to a detailed geometry. So we will perform the clipping in two steps: 1. Clip the raster to the fire perimeter bounding box using [`rio.clip_box()`](https://vylor.github.io/rioxarray/stable/rioxarray.html#rioxarray.raster_array.RasterArray.clip_box) and then 2. Clip the simplified raster to the fire perimeter using [`rio.clip()`](https://vylor.github.io/rioxarray/stable/rioxarray.html#rioxarray.raster_array.RasterArray.clip). Why bother? To clip to a polygon, `rio.clip()` builds a mask with one true/false value per pixel of the raster it receives. Our raster has almost 90,000 x 57,000 pixels, about 5 billion values! Clipping to the bounding box first is fast, because it only selects rows and columns, and it shrinks the raster to about a million pixels before `rio.clip()` builds its mask. ::: {#61c9fe89 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Match CRSs and verify update eaton_match = eaton.to_crs(lulc.rio.crs) assert eaton_match.crs == lulc.rio.crs # Clip large raster to detailed geometry in two steps lulc_step1 = lulc.rio.clip_box(*eaton_match.total_bounds) lulc_step2 = lulc_step1.rio.clip(eaton_match.geometry) # ------------------------------------------------------ fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4)) # Plot the first clipped raster lulc_step1.plot(ax=ax[0]) ax[0].set_title("Step 1: Clip to Bounding Box") ax[0].axis("off") # Plot the second clipped raster lulc_step2.plot(ax=ax[1]) ax[1].set_title("Step 2: Clip to Detailed Geometry") ax[1].axis("off") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-17-raster-wrangling_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){width=621 height=357} ::: ::: We can also do both steps at once using method chaining: ::: {#1c4af0c0 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} lulc_clip = (lulc.rio.clip_box(*eaton_match.total_bounds) .rio.clip(eaton_match.geometry) ) # Examine results lulc_clip.plot() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-17-raster-wrangling_files/figure-html/cell-14-output-1.png){width=588 height=464} ::: ::: ## Areas and CRSs Some of the next exercises ask for areas. Before calculating any area, we need to check that our data is in a CRS where areas make sense: 1. The CRS must be **projected**, so the coordinates are in units of length such as meters, not in degrees. 2. The projection must not distort areas in our region. **Equal-area** projections preserve areas everywhere. Others, like UTM, distort them very little within their zone. Let's start by looking at the raster's CRS: ::: {#bf978af8 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} print('CRS:', lulc.rio.crs) print('Projected:', lulc.rio.crs.is_projected) print('Units:', lulc.rio.crs.linear_units) print('Resolution:', lulc.rio.resolution()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` CRS: EPSG:32611 Projected: True Units: metre Resolution: (10.0, -10.0) ``` ::: ::: The raster is in UTM zone 11N (EPSG:32611), a projected CRS in meters, with 10 m x 10 m pixels. Each pixel covers 10 x 10 = 100 m² on the ground, so we can get areas by counting pixels. UTM is not an equal-area projection, but within its zone the area error is well below 1%: the scale factor goes from 0.9996 at the zone's central meridian to about 1.001 at its edges, and areas change with the square of the scale factor, so they are off by at most about 0.2% @snyder_map_1987. Now the fire perimeter. A `GeoDataFrame`'s CRS: ::: {#99926122 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} eaton.crs ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=111} ``` Name: WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator Axis Info [cartesian]: - X[east]: Easting (metre) - Y[north]: Northing (metre) Area of Use: - name: World between 85.06°S and 85.06°N. - bounds: (-180.0, -85.06, 180.0, 85.06) Coordinate Operation: - name: Popular Visualisation Pseudo-Mercator - method: Popular Visualisation Pseudo Mercator Datum: World Geodetic System 1984 ensemble - Ellipsoid: WGS 84 - Prime Meridian: Greenwich ``` ::: ::: The Eaton perimeter is in EPSG:3857, *WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator*, also called Web Mercator. It is projected and its units are meters, so `.area` will happily return an answer in m². But Web Mercator, the projection used by web maps, preserves shapes and stretches areas more and more the farther we are from the equator. Let's compare the area of the perimeter in its original CRS and in the raster's CRS: ::: {#a1f34c79 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(f"Area in {eaton.crs.name}: {eaton.area.sum() / 1000**2:.1f} km²") print(f"Area in {eaton_match.crs.name}: {eaton_match.area.sum() / 1000**2:.1f} km²") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Area in WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator: 83.4 km² Area in WGS 84 / UTM zone 11N: 56.9 km² ``` ::: ::: At the latitude of Los Angeles, Web Mercator makes areas almost 50% larger! And nothing warned us. :::{.callout-important} Only calculate areas in a projected CRS that preserves areas in your region, such as an equal-area projection or the right UTM zone. Check the CRS in the data itself (`gdf.crs`, `raster.rio.crs`) before trusting an area. ::: ## Categorical or continuous? :::{.callout-tip} ## Check-in Look at the colorbar in the plot of `lulc_clip` we made after clipping. Is land cover *categorical* data (each number is a label for a category) or *continuous* data (each number is a measurement)? What would a pixel with a value of 6 mean? ::: In a categorical raster the numbers are just codes: there is no order and nothing in between two classes. A continuous colormap like the default one suggests both, so a better choice is a **categorical colormap**, with one distinct color per class. The MPC uses an official color for each class of this land cover product, listed in its [class map for `io-lulc-9-class`](https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/data/v1/legend/classmap/io-lulc-9-class). The `labels` data frame we imported at the beginning has, for each class, its code, its name and its official color as a hex code. No Data is fully transparent in the official map, so it gets white: ::: {#55111c0e .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} labels ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=113} ```{=html}
code class_label color
0 0 No Data #ffffff
1 1 Water #419bdf
2 2 Trees #397d49
3 4 Flooded vegetation #7a87c6
4 5 Crops #e49635
5 7 Built area #c4281b
6 8 Bare ground #a59b8f
7 9 Snow/ice #a8ebff
8 10 Clouds #616161
9 11 Rangeland #e3e2c3
``` ::: ::: Notice 0 means "No Data". This is the raster's no-data value we checked before clipping, so in `lulc_clip` the pixels outside the fire perimeter have code 0. To use these colors, we give `.plot()` two lists: - `levels`: the edges between classes. Each class goes from its own code up to the next one (Trees from 2 to 4, Flooded vegetation from 4 to 5, ...), and we add 12 as the last edge. - `colors`: one color per class. Since the colors are now categories, a legend works better than a colorbar. We'll make one entry per class present in the clipped raster: ::: {#3337d88a .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Classes present in the clipped raster (without No Data) present = labels[labels['code'].isin(np.unique(lulc_clip)) & (labels['code'] != 0)] # One legend entry per class # zip() pairs up the colors and names: ('#419bdf', 'Water'), ('#397d49', 'Trees'), ... legend_entries = [] for color, name in zip(present['color'], present['class_label']): legend_entries.append(mpatches.Patch(color=color, label=name)) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5)) lulc_clip.plot(ax=ax, levels=list(labels['code']) + [12], colors=list(labels['color']), add_colorbar=False) ax.legend(handles=legend_entries, loc='upper left', bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1)) ax.set_title('Land cover within the Eaton Fire perimeter (2023)') ax.axis('off') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-17-raster-wrangling_files/figure-html/cell-19-output-1.png){width=751 height=409} ::: ::: ## Land cover statistics In the rest of this lesson we will calculate land cover statistics within the Eaton Fire perimeter. The following exercises will guide you through this process: :::{.callout-tip} ## Exercise 1 1. Use the `numpy` function `np.unique()` to get the number of pixels per class in `lulc_clip`. What other data would you need to know how many buildings were destroyed, or how severely the vegetation burned? ::: ## Class labels from the item's metadata In this lesson we read the class labels and colors from a CSV. In this last section we'll see how to get the class labels from the file itself instead: they are stored in the STAC item's metadata. To extract them, we'll first learn a Python shortcut. ### List comprehensions A **list comprehension** is a short way of writing a `for` loop that builds a new list. #### Example: doubling numbers {.unlisted} Here is a `for` loop that creates a new list by doubling each number in a given list: ::: {#03305035 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4] doubled = [] for n in numbers: doubled.append(n * 2) doubled ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=122} ``` [2, 4, 6, 8] ``` ::: ::: And here is the same thing as a list comprehension: ::: {#11b06cba .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} doubled = [n * 2 for n in numbers] doubled ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=123} ``` [2, 4, 6, 8] ``` ::: ::: Read it from the inside out: "`n * 2` **for** each `n` **in** `numbers`". The square brackets tell Python to collect the results in a new list. Notice everything from the loop is still there (the loop variable `n`, the list `numbers`, and what we do with each element), just in one line. #### Example: one value from each dictionary {.unlisted} Quick recap: a **dictionary** stores *key-value pairs*, written as `{key: value}`. We get a value by putting its key in square brackets. For example, if ```python pet = {'name': 'Tuna', 'age': 5} ``` then `pet['name']` is `'Tuna'` and `pet['age']` is `5`. The following is closer to what we will need in a moment. We have a list of dictionaries and want one value from each: ::: {#b4978b59 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} pets = [{'name': 'Tuna', 'age': 5}, {'name': 'Bowie', 'age': 12}, {'name': 'Momo', 'age': 17}] pet_names = [pet['name'] for pet in pets] pet_names ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=124} ``` ['Tuna', 'Bowie', 'Momo'] ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-tip} ## Check-in 1. Print Momo's age. 2. Use list comprehension to make a list with the ages of the pets. ::: ### Class codes and names Back to our land cover item. The class codes and names are stored in the metadata of the item's `data` asset: ::: {#2ad5b213 .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Class codes and names from the item's metadata class_values = item.assets['data'].extra_fields['file:values'] class_values ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=125} ``` [{'values': [0], 'summary': 'No Data'}, {'values': [1], 'summary': 'Water'}, {'values': [2], 'summary': 'Trees'}, {'values': [4], 'summary': 'Flooded vegetation'}, {'values': [5], 'summary': 'Crops'}, {'values': [7], 'summary': 'Built area'}, {'values': [8], 'summary': 'Bare ground'}, {'values': [9], 'summary': 'Snow/ice'}, {'values': [10], 'summary': 'Clouds'}, {'values': [11], 'summary': 'Rangeland'}] ``` ::: ::: `class_values` is a list of dictionaries, one per class, like `{'values': [0], 'summary': 'No Data'}`. We want two lists out of it: all the codes and all the names. This is a job for a list comprehension! :::{.callout-tip} ## Exercise First, predict the output of each line.
